newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges urgent Mobutu-rebel talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges urgent Mobutu-rebel talks.

text.p: With rebels poised to enter Zaire's capital at any moment, the United States on Tuesday called for President Mobutu Sese Seko to conduct "urgent negotiations" with the rebels on a peaceful transfer of power.
"It seems increasingly apparent the rebel forces will move into the capital. They are very nearby. They are moving quickly," John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, said.

"It is increasingly apparent that President Mobutu or his representatives need to urgently conduct negotiations with the rebel alliance...Our primary concern is a peaceful transfer of power," he said.
"The facts on the ground are beginning to indicate... that there may not be much time here until the transfer of power takes place," he added.
Dinger said negotiations were possible despite the fast-moving rebel advance.

Mobutu, under pressure to quit as rebels closed in on Kinshasa, announced through a spokesman that he would travel to Gabon for an African mini summit on Wednesday and return to his capital two days later.
There was speculation this was part of a deal that would permit Mobutu to leave the capital -- permanently -- before Kabila's rebel forces take over.
U.S. officials said they did not know Mobutu's plans.
Asked at a news briefing if Washington urged Mobutu not to return to Zaire from Gabon, Dinger said:

"The decision by President Mobutu as to what he does, the decision by the rebel alliance regarding President Mobutu's future status, and of course, the decision by the people of Zaire regarding President Mobutu's future there are all decisions for them to make, not for us to make."

The United States has pressed Kabila to establish a transitional government that would include other political opponents as well as his rebel alliance. The ultimate goal is a democratic Zaire set up under free elections.
Dinger noted reports the rebel alliance had taken over the country's railroad and said he hoped Kabila would adhere to earlier statements in support of a market economy.

"There is simply no question here that for Zaire to fulfil its potential -- and that potential is undeniably great -- it does need a free market economy, and it does need a stable government," he said.
"The record shows that a country that follows those two principles receives assistance from the international community, it draws in private investment, and these are the keys to success," he added.
